title: OA 3 — NLP, Generative AI, and Anomaly Detection
description: Mock data-science internship assessment: ensembles, imbalanced learning, embeddings, transformers, RAG and hallucinations; news-sentiment SQL (NewsArticles / Entities / SentimentScores / MarketEvents); text normalisation and entity linking in pandas; heap/top-K and BFS graph DSA.
disclaimer: Independent practice material informed by publicly reported role requirements and general internship-assessment patterns. Not official Nasdaq questions.

revealPolicy.rule: Never send private fields to the candidate's browser; reveal solutions only after the whole attempt has been submitted or timed out.

questions.statement: Why does a random forest usually generalise better than a single deep decision tree trained on the same data?

options.text: Each tree in the forest is shallower, which removes all bias
The forest uses the test set to prune trees
Random forests always have lower training error than a single tree
Averaging many trees trained on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets reduces variance without greatly increasing bias

solution.explanation: Deep trees have low bias but high variance. Bagging plus feature subsampling decorrelates the trees so their averaged prediction is more stable. The forest does not remove bias, never touches the test set, and its training error is not guaranteed to be lower.

questions.statement: Which description of gradient boosting is correct?

options.text: All trees are trained independently in parallel and their votes are averaged
Trees are added sequentially, each one fitted to the current errors (negative gradients) of the ensemble, and a learning rate shrinks each tree's contribution
It trains one very deep tree and then prunes it
Each tree is trained on a different, non-overlapping subset of features only

solution.explanation: Boosting builds an additive model stage by stage to correct previous errors; shrinkage (learning rate) and early stopping control overfitting. Independent training with averaging describes bagging/random forests.

questions.statement: You will cross-validate a classifier on data with 1% positives and want to use SMOTE-style oversampling of the minority class. What is the correct procedure?

options.text: Oversampling is only valid after the final test, never in training
Oversample the whole dataset first, then run cross-validation
Oversample only the training portion inside each fold and evaluate on untouched, original-distribution validation folds
Oversample the validation fold so that it is balanced as well

solution.explanation: If synthetic or duplicated minority samples are created before splitting, copies/neighbours of validation points leak into training and scores are inflated. Validation data must keep the real class distribution.

questions.statement: In a random forest each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of n rows (sampling with replacement). For large n, roughly what fraction of rows is left out of a given tree's sample (and available for out-of-bag evaluation)?

options.text: Exactly 50%
Exactly 0%, since every row is sampled at least once
About 63.2%

solution.explanation: P(a given row is never drawn in n draws) = (1 − 1/n)^n → e^−1 ≈ 0.368. About 63.2% of rows are in the bootstrap sample; the rest provide a built-in validation estimate (OOB error).

questions.statement: A tree ensemble's impurity-based feature importance ranks a high-cardinality ID-like column (thousands of unique values) as the most important feature. What is the best response?

options.text: Treat it with suspicion: impurity importance is biased towards high-cardinality features; check permutation importance on held-out data and consider dropping the identifier
Conclude the identifier is the strongest causal driver of the target
Increase the number of trees until the importance disappears
Standardise the column and re-run the same importance calculation

solution.explanation: Splits on many-valued columns can reduce impurity by chance on training data, inflating impurity-based importance. Permutation importance on validation data measures the loss in performance when the feature is shuffled and is less biased. Importance is not causation.

questions.statement: How does an Isolation Forest decide that a point is anomalous?

options.text: Anomalies are the points farthest from the global mean in every feature
Anomalies are points that the forest classifies with the lowest accuracy
Anomalies are isolated by random splits in fewer steps, so they have shorter average path lengths in the trees
Anomalies are the points with the longest path length in the trees

solution.explanation: Isolation Forest repeatedly splits randomly on features; rare, different points are separated quickly (short paths), while dense normal points need many splits.

questions.statement: 10% of news articles are negative-sentiment. 30% of negative articles contain the word 'lawsuit' versus 5% of non-negative articles. If an article contains 'lawsuit', what is the probability it is negative?

solution.explanation: P(neg|lawsuit) = 0.10·0.30 / (0.10·0.30 + 0.90·0.05) = 0.03/0.075 = 0.40. 30% is the likelihood P(lawsuit|neg), not the posterior.

questions.statement: A sentiment label X takes values −1, 0, +1 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. What is Var(X)?

solution.explanation: E[X] = −0.2 + 0 + 0.3 = 0.1; E[X²] = 0.2 + 0 + 0.3 = 0.5; Var = 0.5 − 0.1² = 0.49. 0.50 forgets to subtract the squared mean.

questions.statement: In a sample of 400 articles, 120 are classified as positive. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the true proportion positive (normal approximation)?

In a 2×2 table of article sentiment (positive/negative) by source type (wire/blog), row totals are 100 (positive) and 300 (negative), column totals are 150 (wire) and 250 (blog), total N = 400. What is the expected count for positive–wire under independence?

solution.explanation: Expected = (row total × column total) / N = 100·150/400 = 37.5. The chi-square statistic sums (O − E)²/E over cells.

questions.statement: A newswire publishes on average 3 articles per hour about a company, modelled as Poisson. What is the probability of seeing no articles in the next hour?

options.text: About 33%
Exactly 0, because the mean is 3
About 95%

solution.explanation: P(N = 0) = e^−λ = e^−3 ≈ 0.0498. About 95% is the probability of at least one article.

questions.statement: Two embedding vectors are u = (3, 4) and v = (4, 3). What is their cosine similarity?

solution.explanation: u·v = 12 + 12 = 24 and |u||v| = 5·5 = 25, so cos = 24/25 = 0.96. It would be 1 only for vectors pointing in the same direction.

questions.statement: Why do transformer models need positional encodings (or equivalent position information)?

options.text: To make attention weights sum to one
Self-attention by itself treats the input as an unordered set, so word order information must be injected explicitly
To allow the model to process only short sentences
To reduce the dimensionality of the embeddings

solution.explanation: Attention computes pairwise interactions without any inherent order, so 'A beat B' and 'B beat A' would look identical without position information. Softmax already normalises attention weights.

questions.statement: A RAG assistant for financial filings sometimes answers with outdated figures even though the correct filing is in the index. Which diagnostic step is most useful first?

options.text: Measure retrieval quality separately (e.g., recall@k of the right passage); if the right chunk is missing from the top-k, fix chunking/metadata filters/reranking before changing the generator
Increase the generator's temperature to get more varied answers
Delete the index and rely only on the model's parametric memory
Fine-tune the model on the questions asked so far, without checking retrieval

solution.explanation: RAG quality depends on both retrieval and generation. If the correct passage is not retrieved, no generator can ground its answer in it; evaluating each stage separately localises the failure. Higher temperature increases randomness, not grounding.

questions.statement: A summarisation model writes a fluent quote attributed to a CEO that does not appear in the source article. Which mitigation is most appropriate for a production newsroom tool?

options.text: Ground generation in the source, require citations/quote verification against the text, and keep a human review step for high-stakes outputs
Set temperature to 0, which guarantees that hallucinations cannot occur
Remove all source documents so the model relies on its own knowledge
Make the prompt longer and more polite

solution.explanation: Hallucinated content is plausible but unsupported. Lower temperature can reduce variability but offers no guarantee; grounding, automated checks against sources and human oversight address the risk.

questions.statement: Scores in descending order are 90, 90, 80. Which window function assigns the ranks 1, 1, 2 respectively?

options.text: RANK()
NTILE(3)
DENSE_RANK()
ROW_NUMBER()

solution.explanation: DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same rank without gaps (1,1,2). RANK leaves a gap after ties (1,1,3); ROW_NUMBER numbers rows uniquely (1,2,3).

questions.statement: An article can mention many entities and an entity can appear in many articles, with a sentiment score per mention. What is the standard relational design?

options.text: Duplicate the article text for each entity in the Entities table
Store a comma-separated list of entity ids in an Articles column
A junction table (article_id, entity_id, score) with a composite primary key (article_id, entity_id) and foreign keys to both parents
Add one entity_id column to Articles

solution.explanation: Many-to-many relationships are modelled with an associative table keyed by both foreign keys; lists in a column violate first normal form and make joins and constraints hard.
`remove(1)` with an int literal resolves to `remove(int index)`, deleting the element at index 1 (20). To remove the value 1 you would call `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))`.

options.text: BA
AB
A
B

solution.explanation: A subclass constructor implicitly calls `super()` first, so the superclass constructor body runs before the subclass constructor body.

questions.statement: A unit test for a function that computes a daily sentiment average calls a live sentiment API over the network. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Replace the API with a stub/mock returning fixed values so the test is fast, deterministic and independent of the network
Test only that the function does not throw an exception
Delete the test because networks are unreliable
Keep the live call and re-run the test until it passes

solution.explanation: Unit tests should isolate the unit under test. Stubbing the external dependency makes results repeatable, so assertions about the calculation are meaningful.

questions.statement: Cell A2 contains "  Fed holds rates steady " (extra spaces at both ends). What does =LEN(TRIM(A2))-LEN(SUBSTITUTE(TRIM(A2)," ",""))+1 return?

solution.explanation: TRIM leaves "Fed holds rates steady" (22 characters, 3 spaces); removing spaces leaves 19 characters; 22 − 19 + 1 = 4 words.

questions.statement: On an earnings-news day a stock returned +3.0% while the market index returned +2.2%. The stock's beta is 1.2. Using a simple market model (expected return = beta × market return, risk-free rate ignored), what is the abnormal return?

solution.explanation: Expected return = 1.2 × 2.2% = 2.64%. Abnormal return = actual − expected = 3.00% − 2.64% = 0.36%. +0.80% ignores beta (3.0 − 2.2); +3.0% ignores market movement.

questions.title: Confidence-Weighted Company Sentiment
questions.statement:
An NLP pipeline stores one sentiment score per (article, entity). Using `SentimentScores` and `Entities`, build a leaderboard of **companies** (`entity_type = 'COMPANY'`).

Only use scores with `confidence >= 0.5`. For each company return:

`entity_name, ticker, n_mentions, weighted_score, min_score`

* `n_mentions` – number of qualifying scores
* `weighted_score` – confidence-weighted mean `SUM(score * confidence) / SUM(confidence)` rounded to 3 decimals
* `min_score` – the lowest qualifying `score`

Keep companies with **at least 2** qualifying scores. Sort by `weighted_score` descending, then `entity_name` ascending.

tables.name: Entities
tables.description: Companies, people and sectors recognised in text.

tables.name: SentimentScores
tables.description: Sentiment of an article towards an entity (one row per article/entity pair).

questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE NewsArticles (
  article_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  headline     TEXT NOT NULL,
  source       TEXT NOT NULL,
  published_at TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  language     TEXT NOT NULL           -- ISO code, e.g. 'en'
);
CREATE TABLE Entities (
  entity_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  entity_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  entity_type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (entity_type IN ('COMPANY','PERSON','SECTOR')),
  ticker      TEXT                      -- NULL for non-companies
);
CREATE TABLE SentimentScores (
  article_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES NewsArticles(article_id),
  entity_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Entities(entity_id),
  score      REAL NOT NULL CHECK (score BETWEEN -1 AND 1),
  confidence REAL NOT NULL CHECK (confidence BETWEEN 0 AND 1),
  PRIMARY KEY (article_id, entity_id)
);
CREATE TABLE MarketEvents (
  event_id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  entity_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Entities(entity_id),
  event_time    TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  event_type    TEXT NOT NULL,
  magnitude_pct REAL NOT NULL           -- signed price move in percent
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT e.entity_name, e.ticker, COUNT(*) AS n_mentions, 0.0 AS weighted_score, MIN(s.score) AS min_score
FROM SentimentScores s
JOIN Entities e ON e.entity_id = s.entity_id
-- TODO: filters, HAVING, ORDER BY
GROUP BY e.entity_id, e.entity_name, e.ticker;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: entity_name, ticker, n_mentions, weighted_score, min_score. Order: weighted_score DESC, entity_name ASC.

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT e.entity_name, e.ticker,
       COUNT(*) AS n_mentions,
       ROUND(SUM(s.score * s.confidence) / SUM(s.confidence), 3) AS weighted_score,
       MIN(s.score) AS min_score
FROM SentimentScores s
JOIN Entities e ON e.entity_id = s.entity_id
WHERE e.entity_type = 'COMPANY' AND s.confidence >= 0.5
GROUP BY e.entity_id, e.entity_name, e.ticker
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY weighted_score DESC, e.entity_name ASC;
solution.explanation: WHERE removes low-confidence scores and non-companies before grouping; the weighted mean divides the confidence-weighted sum by total confidence; HAVING keeps companies with >= 2 qualifying rows.

rubric.formula: earned = 200 * (sum of weights of passed tests) / (sum of all test weights)
rules: A submission that only compiles/executes without matching expected output earns 0 for that test.

Low-confidence rows must be filtered before aggregation (WHERE, not HAVING).

questions.title: Daily Sentiment Momentum
questions.statement:
Using `NewsArticles`, `SentimentScores` and `Entities`, compute day-over-day sentiment momentum for **English** articles only (`language = 'en'`).

For each entity and calendar day (`DATE(published_at)`) that has at least one English score, return:

`entity_name, day, n_scores, avg_score, change_from_prev`

* `n_scores` – number of scores that day
* `avg_score` – average `score`, rounded to 3 decimals
* `change_from_prev` – `avg_score` minus the entity's `avg_score` on its **previous day that has data**, rounded to 3 decimals; `NULL` for the entity's first day

Sort by `entity_name`, then `day`.

CREATE TABLE Entities (

  ticker      TEXT                      -- NULL for non-companies

CREATE TABLE SentimentScores (

  score      REAL NOT NULL CHECK (score BETWEEN -1 AND 1),

);
CREATE TABLE MarketEvents (
  event_id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,

  event_type    TEXT NOT NULL,
  magnitude_pct REAL NOT NULL           -- signed price move in percent
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT e.entity_name, DATE(a.published_at) AS day, COUNT(*) AS n_scores, 0.0 AS avg_score, NULL AS change_from_prev
FROM NewsArticles a
JOIN SentimentScores s ON s.article_id = a.article_id
JOIN Entities e ON e.entity_id = s.entity_id
GROUP BY e.entity_name, DATE(a.published_at);
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: entity_name, day (YYYY-MM-DD text), n_scores, avg_score, change_from_prev. Order: entity_name, day.

solution.referenceSolution:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT e.entity_name, DATE(a.published_at) AS day,
         COUNT(*) AS n_scores, ROUND(AVG(s.score), 3) AS avg_score
  FROM NewsArticles a
  JOIN SentimentScores s ON s.article_id = a.article_id
  JOIN Entities e        ON e.entity_id  = s.entity_id
  WHERE a.language = 'en'
  GROUP BY e.entity_id, e.entity_name, DATE(a.published_at)
)
SELECT entity_name, day, n_scores, avg_score,
       ROUND(avg_score - LAG(avg_score) OVER (PARTITION BY entity_name ORDER BY day), 3) AS change_from_prev
FROM daily
ORDER BY entity_name, day;
solution.explanation: Aggregate to entity-day first in a CTE, then apply LAG over the aggregated rows partitioned by entity and ordered by day. Applying LAG before grouping would compare individual articles instead of daily averages.

Gaps in days: the previous *available* day is used.

questions.starterQuery:
UPDATE SentimentScores
SET confidence = confidence + 0.1
WHERE 1 = 0;  -- TODO: EXISTS (confirming event within 24h); cap at 1.0
questions.outputSpec: Final contents of SentimentScores, NewsArticles and MarketEvents are compared with the expected post-update state (confidence tolerance 1e-6).

checkQueries.sql: SELECT * FROM SentimentScores ORDER BY article_id, entity_id
SELECT * FROM MarketEvents ORDER BY event_id
SELECT * FROM NewsArticles ORDER BY article_id

solution.referenceSolution:
UPDATE SentimentScores
SET confidence = ROUND(MIN(1.0, confidence + 0.1), 2)
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM NewsArticles a
  JOIN MarketEvents m ON m.entity_id = SentimentScores.entity_id
  WHERE a.article_id = SentimentScores.article_id
    AND m.event_time >= a.published_at
    AND m.event_time <= DATETIME(a.published_at, '+1 day')
    AND ((SentimentScores.score > 0 AND m.magnitude_pct > 0) OR (SentimentScores.score < 0 AND m.magnitude_pct < 0))
);
solution.explanation: A correlated EXISTS subquery joins the article (for published_at) to market events of the same entity. Because EXISTS yields a boolean, multiple confirming events cannot double-boost. MIN(1.0, x) inside ROUND caps the value; DATETIME(published_at, '+1 day') computes the window end.

questions.title: Normalise and Deduplicate Headlines
questions.statement:
Implement `normalize_headlines(articles)` to prepare headlines for NLP.

1. Parse `published_at` with format `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S` (invalid → NaT). Drop rows with a missing `headline` or an invalid `published_at`.
2. Create `headline_norm`: lower-case the headline, replace every run of characters other than `a-z` and `0-9` with a single space, and strip leading/trailing spaces. Drop rows whose `headline_norm` is empty.
3. Rows with the same `headline_norm` are duplicates. Keep the one with the **earliest** `published_at` (tie → smallest `article_id`) and record `n_duplicates` = number of *other* rows collapsed into it (int64).
4. Return `article_id, headline_norm, published_at, n_duplicates`, sorted by `published_at` then `article_id`, with default index.
questions.starterCode:
import pandas as pd

def normalize_headlines(articles: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = articles.copy()
    # TODO
    return df
questions.outputSpec: Columns [article_id int64, headline_norm str, published_at datetime64, n_duplicates int64].

comparison.dtypePolicy: Values compared by category: numeric (int/float interchangeable), bool, datetime, str; nulls (NaN/NaT/None/pd.NA) equal each other.

publicTests.description: Sample: punctuation, case, duplicates with ties, missing values

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def normalize_headlines(articles):
    df = articles.copy()
    df["published_at"] = pd.to_datetime(df["published_at"], format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["headline", "published_at"])
    df["headline_norm"] = (df["headline"].str.lower()
                           .str.replace(r"[^a-z0-9]+", " ", regex=True).str.strip())
    df = df[df["headline_norm"] != ""]
    df = df.sort_values(["headline_norm", "published_at", "article_id"], kind="mergesort")
    sizes = df.groupby("headline_norm")["article_id"].transform("size")
    df["n_duplicates"] = (sizes - 1).astype("int64")
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="headline_norm", keep="first")
    df = df.sort_values(["published_at", "article_id"], kind="mergesort")
    return df[["article_id", "headline_norm", "published_at", "n_duplicates"]].reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: Vectorised string cleaning with str.lower + regex replace; sort so the desired survivor comes first, compute group sizes via transform('size'), then drop_duplicates(keep='first').

questions.title: Entity Linking by Normalised Aliases
questions.statement:
Implement `match_entities(mentions, aliases)` to link text spans to entity ids.

Define a *key* for any text: lower-case; replace each run of non-`[a-z0-9]` characters by one space; strip; then **repeatedly remove a trailing company suffix word** from `{inc, corp, corporation, ltd, plc, co}` (only when it is preceded by another word – a text that is just `inc` keeps its key `inc`).

1. Compute keys for `mentions.text_span` and for `aliases.alias`.
2. If several aliases share a key, keep only the one with the **smallest `entity_id`**.
3. Left-join mentions to the alias table on the key.
4. `entity_id` is a nullable integer (`Int64`) – `<NA>` for unmatched mentions; `matched` is a bool.

Return `mention_id, article_id, entity_id, matched` sorted by `mention_id`, default index.

comparison.dtypePolicy: Values compared by category: numeric (int/float interchangeable), bool, datetime, str; nulls (NaN/NaT/None/pd.NA) equal each other.

publicTests.description: Sample: suffix stripping, ambiguous alias, unmatched
Aliases that normalise to the same key keep the smallest entity_id

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

SUFFIX = r"(?:\s+(?:inc|corp|corporation|ltd|plc|co))+$"

def _norm(s):
    s = s.str.lower().str.replace(r"[^a-z0-9]+", " ", regex=True).str.strip()
    return s.str.replace(SUFFIX, "", regex=True)

def match_entities(mentions, aliases):
    m = mentions.copy()
    a = aliases.copy()
    m["key"] = _norm(m["text_span"])
    a["key"] = _norm(a["alias"])
    a = a.sort_values(["key", "entity_id"]).drop_duplicates("key", keep="first")[["key", "entity_id"]]
    out = m.merge(a, on="key", how="left")
    out["entity_id"] = out["entity_id"].astype("Int64")
    out["matched"] = out["entity_id"].notna()
    return out.sort_values("mention_id")[["mention_id", "article_id", "entity_id", "matched"]].reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: Normalise both sides with the same vectorised function, deduplicate aliases on the key (smallest entity_id), merge with how='left' and cast entity_id to the nullable Int64 type so missing links stay missing rather than becoming floats.

questions.title: Six-Hour Sentiment Bins
questions.statement:
Implement `six_hour_sentiment(scores)`.

1. Parse `published_at` (`%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`, invalid → NaT) and drop rows with an invalid timestamp or a missing `score`.
2. If a `(article_id, entity_id)` pair repeats, keep the **last** occurrence in input order.
3. Assign each row to a 6-hour bin: `bin_start = published_at.floor('6h')`.
4. For each `(entity_id, bin_start)` compute `mean_score`, `n_articles` (distinct `article_id`) and `max_abs_score` (largest absolute score).
5. Return `entity_id, bin_start, mean_score, n_articles, max_abs_score` sorted by `entity_id`, `bin_start`; only bins that contain data appear.

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def six_hour_sentiment(scores):
    df = scores.copy()
    df["published_at"] = pd.to_datetime(df["published_at"], format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["published_at", "score"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["article_id", "entity_id"], keep="last")
    df["bin_start"] = df["published_at"].dt.floor("6h")
    out = (df.groupby(["entity_id", "bin_start"], as_index=False)
             .agg(mean_score=("score", "mean"), n_articles=("article_id", "nunique"), max_abs_score=("score", lambda s: s.abs().max())))
    return out.sort_values(["entity_id", "bin_start"]).reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: Coerce timestamps, drop invalid rows, dedupe with keep='last', floor to 6h and use groupby with named aggregation; nunique counts distinct articles.

questions.title: Top-K Most Influential Entities
questions.statement:
A news-analytics service receives a list of `[entity_name, weight]` events (a weight is an integer influence score and can be negative). The total influence of an entity is the sum of its weights.

Return the names of the **k entities with the largest total influence**, ordered from largest to smallest total. If two entities have the same total, the one whose name is **lexicographically smaller** (plain string comparison, case-sensitive) comes first.

examples.description: ACME has total 7, CIRRUS 7, BANK 5: tie on 7 broken alphabetically
All three tie on 5; names a, b, c come first alphabetically

solution.referenceSolution:
import heapq
from typing import List
from collections import defaultdict

def top_k_entities(events: List[List], k: int) -> List[str]:
    total = defaultdict(int)
    for name, weight in events:
        total[name] += weight
    best = heapq.nsmallest(k, total.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
    return [name for name, _ in best]
solution.explanation: Aggregate totals in a hash map, then select the k best with a heap (heapq.nsmallest with key (-total, name)). The key encodes both the ordering and the tie-break.

questions.title: Reliable Relay Routes
questions.statement:
A knowledge graph links `n` entities (numbered `0..n-1`). Each undirected link `[u, v, conf]` has a confidence value. Only links with `conf >= min_conf` may be used.

Return `[hops, routes]` where `hops` is the minimum number of links needed to travel from `src` to `dst` and `routes` is the **number of distinct shortest routes** modulo `1_000_000_007`. A route is a sequence of links, so parallel links between the same pair of entities give distinct routes. If `dst` cannot be reached return `[-1, 0]`; if `src == dst` return `[0, 1]`.
constraints: 0 <= u, v < n, u != v; parallel links are allowed

examples.description: Link 3-4 has confidence 2 < 5, so node 4 is unreachable
